Another field view of Notonecta glauca with the upside-down hunting body plan and compact, boat-like outline visible from above.

hero.lede: Common Backswimmer is one of the best pond insects for noticing that the water surface is a hunting layer, not just a boundary. It hangs upside down below the film, carries a silvery air store over the body, and can detect the ripples made by struggling prey.
hero.shortMorphology: A pale olive-brown backswimmer with a dark central wing patch, large reddish eyes and long hair-fringed hind legs that work like oars; living adults often look silvery because air is trapped along the body.

internationalContext.summary: Common Backswimmer is unusually good for explaining how an aquatic insect hunts at the air-water interface. DOI-backed studies show that it detects prey-generated ripples, changes prey choice with water depth and oxygen conditions, carries a persistent air layer on the body, and combines strong underwater and aerial visual performance. A separate global IUCN Red List assessment is not cited here.

world.label: No separate global assessment cited
world.note: A separate global IUCN assessment is not cited here.

ecology: It can discriminate prey from non-prey by the frequency pattern of water-surface waves, which helps explain why the species spends so much time poised just under the surface film.
Prey choice changes with depth: shallow water makes benthic prey more profitable, while deeper water pushes foraging back toward surface prey because diving costs rise.
Dissolved oxygen and temperature change how long the insect can stay submerged and which prey types overlap most with its hunting zone.
The body surface is strongly superhydrophobic and retains a durable air layer, supporting both respiration and reduced wetting under water.
Its visual system is flexible enough for both submerged hunting and flight, which fits a species that must work in two optical environments.
threats: No global IUCN threat category is cited here; the species is more often treated as a common freshwater predator than as a current international red-list priority.
Even a widespread backswimmer depends on pond conditions that keep hunting profitable, because oxygen regime and water depth directly affect how it can use different prey layers.
Open-data maps can exaggerate security in heavily recorded countries and understate occupancy where freshwater insects are simply less often reported.

phenology.northernEurope: Adults are active through the warmer part of the year in ponds, ditches and other still waters, especially when sunny conditions bring them close to the surface and encourage dispersal between water bodies.
phenology.note: Warm, bright weather often makes surface activity easiest to see.

swedishContext.summary: In Sweden, Artfakta/Dyntaxa treats Notonecta glauca as accepted and allmän ryggsimmare as the recommended Swedish name. The local 2025 Swedish Red List workbook keeps the species in LC and describes it as resident and reproducing. That makes it a useful Swedish teaching species: common enough to encounter, but still rich in behavior once you watch the water surface closely.

redList2025.documentation: De skattade värdena som bedömningen baserar sig på ligger alla inom intervallet för kategorin Livskraftig (LC).

keyFacts: Artfakta/Dyntaxa taxon 226119 treats Notonecta glauca as accepted and allmän ryggsimmare as the recommended Swedish name.
The Swedish Red List 2025 row classifies the species as LC rather than as a current Swedish conservation priority.
The same Swedish source describes the species as resident and reproducing in Sweden.
The linked Uppsala photos fit a species that should be searched for in ordinary still-water habitats rather than only in unusual specialist sites.
